findings.title: High-Frequency Road Noise
findings.where: Road screen, the asphalt/dirt texture surrounding the lane markings
findings.problem: The ground texture is composed of harsh, high-contrast pixel noise (salt-and-pepper effect). It lacks a solid mid-tone base, creating visual vibration that competes with the vehicle and lane dividers.
findings.why: In a top-down driver, peripheral vision tracks the ground to gauge speed and lateral position. This texture causes immediate eye strain and makes the car visually 'sink' into the floor.
findings.fix: Apply a Gaussian blur to the source texture or reduce the noise frequency by 80%. Overlay a dark, semi-transparent solid color to establish a base value, ensuring the lane markings pop with higher contrast.

findings.title: Monospace Data Dump
findings.where: Constructor screen, left-hand component list (Name, Chassis, Weapon slots)
findings.problem: The entire list uses a uniform monospace font, size, and color weight. There is no visual distinction between category headers (e.g., 'Armor: Front') and interactive values (e.g., '0' or '(empty)').
findings.why: It forces the player to read every character linearly to find an empty slot or understand the structure. It feels like a developer debug console rather than a user-friendly garage interface, slowing down the creative loop.
findings.fix: Switch labels to a lighter-weight, non-monospace sans-serif grey. Bold the values. Add subtle alternating row background colors (zebra striping) to guide the eye horizontally across the label-value pairs.

findings.title: Obvious Ground Tiling
findings.where: City screen, the cracked-earth ground texture covering the play area
findings.problem: The ground texture repeats on a strict orthogonal grid with visible seams and repeating crack patterns. Combined with the flat, unshaded building sprites, the scene resembles a 2D level editor rather than a rendered world.
findings.why: It shatters the immersion of the 'Open World.' The rigid, repetitive geometry draws attention away from the gameplay (the car and navigation) and highlights the technical limitations of the art assets.
findings.fix: Implement a larger texture atlas or blend two overlapping textures with different scales to break the pattern. Add a radial gradient overlay (vignette) centered on the car to darken the edges and hide the repetition at the periphery.

findings.title: Logo/UI Value Clash
findings.where: Title screen, center overlay (Logo and Menu)
findings.problem: The 'SMDUEL' logo text and the menu container border share the exact same neon cyan hue and similar luminance. They vibrate against each other, flattening the depth between the branding and the interactive interface.
findings.why: The player's eye does not know where to rest. The lack of value difference between the 'atmospheric' element (title) and the 'functional' element (menu) weakens the call to action and looks amateurish.
findings.fix: Darken the menu background fill significantly (to >90% opacity black) to create a distinct 'window' over the artwork. Desaturate the title text slightly or add a heavy drop shadow to push it visually behind the menu plane.

findings.title: Cramped Condition Panel
findings.where: Arena and Road screens, top-right 'CONDITION' panel
findings.problem: The panel packs armor values, tire health, and driver status into a very small area with tiny fonts and miniature +/- buttons. The critical red 'Body armor' warning is lost in the dense text block.
findings.why: Players need to assess their status in a split second during combat. Currently, they must stop looking at the road to decipher the tiny text, increasing cognitive load and delaying reaction times to damage.
findings.fix: Remove the incremental adjustment buttons from the active HUD (reserve them for the pause menu). Convert the numeric armor values into horizontal bar graphs (matching the existing Tire bars) for instant shape-recognition. Increase vertical padding between the Armor, Tyres, and Driver sections.
